name: Computer Networks
description: Understand and trace a network from framing and medium access through IP, transport, security and distributed applications, using original calculations and protocol scenarios grounded in the supplied course archive.
limitations: Based on supplied CSE14B/CSE1405 teaching materials, not current product recommendations or examination regulations.
All exercises are newly authored practice. Open responses are ungraded and require review against their rubrics.
Historical Ethernet, TCP Tahoe/Reno, simplified handshakes and toy cryptography are explicitly teaching models, not claims about every deployed implementation.
No packet captures, physical labs, external recordings or live network experiments were run. Scenario traces are analytical exercises.

Source PDFs were text-inspected with sampled visual checks, not exhaustively reviewed diagram by diagram. Student summaries were treated as secondary and corrected where they conflict with precise protocol reasoning.

Decimal network rates use 1000-based prefixes; byte/bit conversions and omitted overhead are stated in calculation prompts. Cryptographic examples with tiny keys or toy ciphers are for arithmetic only.

topics.name: Layering, encapsulation and delay
topics.description: Track what each layer provides and distinguish rate from latency.

skills.name: Trace a layered exchange
skills.description: Separate service interfaces, peer protocols and encapsulation.

skills.name: Calculate delay and capacity
skills.description: Account for serialization, propagation, store-and-forward and units.

lesson.title: Services and protocols
paragraphs: A layer offers a service to the layer above through an interface. A protocol specifies the rules followed by corresponding layers on different machines. The apparent peer-to-peer exchange is implemented by passing data down the local stack, across links, and up the remote stack. A TCP byte stream can be carried inside IP packets inside link frames without applications implementing every lower-layer detail.

The OSI order is physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation, application. The Internet teaching stack often combines the upper three and sometimes combines physical/link. A normal IP router forwards using network-layer information and replaces the link encapsulation at each hop; it does not terminate every passing TCP connection. Connection-oriented and reliable are distinct properties, not synonyms.

lesson.title: Follow the last bit
paragraphs: Serialization time is L/R for L bits at rate R bits/s. Propagation time is distance/signal speed and does not grow with packet length. End-to-end delay also includes processing and queuing. Under store-and-forward a router waits for the whole packet before transmitting it on the next link, so serialization delays add for one packet.

Worked example: a 1500-byte packet takes 12000/1,000,000=12 ms on a 1 Mb/s link. Two identical store-and-forward links with 5 ms propagation each take 12+5+12+5=34 ms, ignoring queues and processing. The bandwidth-delay product R*T counts bits in flight for the chosen one-way or round-trip T; explicitly distinguish those choices.

exercises.title: Serialization units
exercises.prompt: A 1500-byte packet crosses a 1 Mb/s link. With 1 Mb/s=1,000,000 bits/s and no framing overhead, what is serialization time in integer milliseconds?

exercises.title: Propagation distance
exercises.prompt: A link is 200 km long and signal speed is 200,000 km/s. What is one-way propagation delay in milliseconds?
exercises.explanation: 200/200000 seconds=0.001 seconds=1 ms.

exercises.title: Two store-and-forward links
exercises.prompt: A single packet takes 12 ms to serialize on each of two links. Each link adds 5 ms propagation. The router uses store-and-forward; queues and processing are zero. When does the final bit arrive, in ms after transmission starts?
exercises.explanation: The final bit must finish both serializations and both propagations: 12+5+12+5=34.

exercises.title: Rate versus delay
exercises.prompt: Doubling the rate of a fixed-length link changes neither its length nor signal speed. Which delay is directly halved for a fixed packet?
exercises.explanation: Serialization L/R halves; propagation distance/speed is unchanged. Queuing depends on traffic.

exercises.title: Router responsibilities
exercises.prompt: Explain what link-layer information normally changes when a router forwards an IPv4 packet onto a different Ethernet link, and which destination identifies the remote host.
exercises.explanation: The router removes the incoming frame and creates a new frame with next-hop link addresses. The IP destination identifies the remote host, barring translation; TTL and header checksum also change on IPv4 forwarding.
rubric: Describe per-hop frame replacement.
Distinguish next-hop MAC destination from end-host IP destination.
Avoid claiming the entire IP header stays unchanged.

exercises.title: Protocol versus service
exercises.prompt: An application calls send() on a socket while TCP endpoints exchange acknowledgments. Identify which action is an interface/service use and which is a peer protocol action.
exercises.explanation: send() invokes the local transport service through an interface. TCP acknowledgments are protocol messages exchanged between transport peers.
rubric: Classify the local API call.
Classify the remote peer exchange.

exercises.title: Round-trip pipe capacity
exercises.prompt: A path sustains 2,000,000 bits/s and has propagation RTT 40 ms. Ignoring all overhead, how many bytes equal rate times this RTT?
exercises.explanation: 2,000,000*0.04=80,000 bits; divide by 8 for 10,000 bytes.

exercises.title: Layer ordering
exercises.prompt: Which order runs upward through the first four OSI layers?
exercises.explanation: Bits cross the physical medium, frames one link, packets the network, and transport serves processes end to end.

topics.name: Framing, error detection and correction
topics.description: Encode boundaries, calculate checksums and distinguish detection from correction.

skills.name: Frame and detect corruption
skills.description: Trace stuffing, parity, one's-complement checksums and CRC division.

skills.name: Reason about error-correcting codes
skills.description: Use minimum distance, parity positions and Hamming syndromes.

lesson.title: Boundaries and redundant checks
paragraphs: A receiver needs to distinguish payload from frame delimiters. Byte stuffing escapes reserved flag and escape bytes; bit stuffing inserts a zero after a specified run of ones so the delimiter cannot occur in encoded data. The run length is protocol-specific: use the convention stated in the exercise, not a memorized value from a different example.

Even parity detects any odd number of bit flips but can miss an even number. An Internet-style checksum adds fixed-width words with end-around carry and complements the result; real Internet checksum words are 16 bits, while small worked examples use fewer. For 4-bit words 1010 and 1100, the sum 10110 wraps to 0111, and the checksum is 1000. CRC treats bits as polynomial coefficients over GF(2): append r zeros for a degree-r generator, divide using XOR, and append the r-bit remainder.

lesson.title: Correction requires distance
paragraphs: If valid codewords have minimum Hamming distance d, up to d-1 bit errors are guaranteed detectable, and floor((d-1)/2) are guaranteed correctable. A single-error-correcting Hamming code with m data bits and r parity bits needs 2^r>=m+r+1 to distinguish no error and each possible flipped position.

Place parity bits at positions 1,2,4,... counting from one; parity bit 2^j covers positions whose binary index contains that bit. Specify even or odd parity and data ordering. A syndrome names the flipped position under the single-error assumption. Plain Hamming correction can miscorrect multiple errors; extended Hamming adds an overall parity bit to support single-error correction and double-error detection.

exercises.title: Even parity bit
exercises.prompt: Append one even-parity bit to data 1011001. What is the parity bit, as integer 0 or 1?
exercises.explanation: The data already contain four ones, so append zero to keep an even total.

exercises.title: Checksum with carry
exercises.prompt: Use 4-bit one's-complement arithmetic. Add words 1010 and 1100, wrap the carry, and complement. Which checksum results?
exercises.explanation: 10+12=22=10110; wrap 1 into 0110 to get 0111, then complement to 1000.

exercises.title: CRC remainder
exercises.prompt: Encode data bits 1101 with CRC generator 1011 (degree 3). Append three zeros and divide using XOR. Which three-bit remainder is appended?

exercises.title: Stuff a run
exercises.prompt: In this exercise insert a zero immediately after every five consecutive payload ones, resetting the run counter after insertion. How many stuffed zeros are added to ten consecutive ones? Exclude frame delimiters.
exercises.explanation: Each group of five payload ones triggers one zero, yielding 111110111110.

exercises.title: Hamming parity count
exercises.prompt: How many parity bits r are minimally needed for single-error-correcting Hamming encoding of nine data bits, using 2^r>=9+r+1?
exercises.explanation: r=3 gives 8<13; r=4 gives 16>=14. The code has 13 total bits.

exercises.title: Minimum distance
exercises.prompt: A block code has minimum Hamming distance 5. How many arbitrary bit errors can it guarantee to correct?
exercises.explanation: floor((5-1)/2)=2; detection and correction guarantees differ.

exercises.title: Decode a syndrome
exercises.prompt: In an even-parity Hamming(7,4) code, checks at positions 1 and 4 fail while the check at 2 passes. Assuming at most one bit error, which one-based bit position should be flipped?
exercises.explanation: The syndrome is 4+1=5, binary 101. This locates an error only under the stated assumption.

exercises.title: Two-dimensional parity blind spot
exercises.prompt: A data block has even parity on every row and column. Explain why flipping four data bits at the corners of a rectangle can evade all those parity checks.
exercises.explanation: Each affected row has exactly two flips and each affected column has exactly two. Both preserve parity, so all checks remain satisfied despite corrupted data.
rubric: Identify two flips in each affected row.
Identify two in each affected column.
Conclude that passing parity is not proof of correctness.

topics.name: ARQ and sliding windows
topics.description: Trace loss recovery and calculate a useful window size.

skills.name: Trace acknowledgments and retransmission
skills.description: Handle lost data/ACKs, duplicates and receiver buffering.

skills.name: Calculate window efficiency
skills.description: Derive timing cycles and sequence-space constraints.

lesson.title: Reliable delivery needs identity
paragraphs: Stop-and-wait sends one frame, then waits for acknowledgment. A timer permits retransmission after loss, but without sequence numbers a lost ACK can cause duplicate delivery. Alternating-bit sequence numbers let the receiver acknowledge a duplicate while discarding its repeated payload.

Go-Back-N normally accepts only the next expected frame and uses cumulative ACKs; after loss, subsequent frames may need retransmission. Selective Repeat buffers valid out-of-order frames and acknowledges individual arrivals, retransmitting missing frames. Always define whether an ACK number means the last accepted frame or the next expected frame; both conventions appear in teaching diagrams.

lesson.title: Window arithmetic and timing
paragraphs: With data serialization T, one-way propagation p, ACK serialization A and no processing/queueing, a stop-and-wait cycle is T+2p+A. Its sender utilization is T/(T+2p+A). Under ideal pipelining, a window W can fill the link if W*T covers the ACK-return cycle; account for exact event timing when equality occurs.

For a k-bit sequence number, the space has 2^k labels. Standard Go-Back-N with receiver window one permits sender window at most 2^k-1. Selective Repeat with equal sender/receiver windows requires W<=2^(k-1), preventing a delayed old frame from looking like a new one after wraparound. For k=3 these limits are 7 and 4, respectively.

exercises.title: Stop-and-wait cycle
exercises.prompt: A data frame takes 2 ms to serialize; one-way propagation is 9 ms. ACK serialization and all other delays are zero. How long is one stop-and-wait cycle in ms?
exercises.explanation: 2+9+9=20 ms from starting the data frame to receiving its ACK.

exercises.title: Utilization
exercises.prompt: Using a 2 ms data serialization time and 20 ms complete stop-and-wait cycle, with no errors, what fraction of time is the sender transmitting data?
exercises.explanation: Data transmission occupies 2/20=0.1 of the cycle.

exercises.title: Window to fill the path
exercises.prompt: Frames take 2 ms to serialize. The first frame's ACK returns 20 ms after its transmission starts. ACKs then return every 2 ms; no loss or other limits apply. What minimum sender window in frames prevents idle time?
exercises.explanation: Ten frames occupy [0,20] ms. At 20 ms the first ACK frees a slot, so transmission can continue.

exercises.title: Selective Repeat limit
exercises.prompt: Selective Repeat uses 4-bit sequence numbers and equal sender/receiver windows. What is the maximum safe window in the standard no-ambiguity model?
exercises.explanation: Half of the 16 sequence labels can be in a window: W<=2^(4-1)=8.

exercises.title: Go-Back-N limit
exercises.prompt: Standard Go-Back-N uses 4-bit frame sequence numbers and receiver window one. What is its maximum sender window?
exercises.explanation: Leave one label outside the active window: 2^4-1=15.

exercises.title: Lost acknowledgment
exercises.prompt: In alternating-bit stop-and-wait, frame 0 is delivered but its ACK is lost. The sender retransmits frame 0. Describe the receiver's correct action.
exercises.explanation: The receiver recognizes the old sequence number, does not deliver the payload twice, and sends the acknowledgment again so the sender can progress.
rubric: Detect a duplicate using sequence state.
Avoid duplicate delivery.
Re-acknowledge rather than silently discard forever.

exercises.title: Different loss recovery
exercises.prompt: Frames 0,1,2,3 are sent; frame 1 is lost and 2,3 arrive. Compare textbook Go-Back-N and Selective Repeat receiver behavior, assuming sufficient windows and no other errors.
exercises.explanation: Go-Back-N discards out-of-order 2 and 3 and keeps indicating the missing 1; recovery retransmits 1 and subsequent outstanding frames. Selective Repeat buffers 2 and 3 and acknowledges them; after retransmitting 1 it can deliver the contiguous sequence.
rubric: Explain discard versus buffering.
Explain cumulative versus individual acknowledgment behavior.
Identify which frames need retransmission.

exercises.title: Include ACK serialization
exercises.prompt: A 1000-bit frame and 100-bit ACK use separate directions of a full-duplex 100,000 bit/s link. One-way propagation is 5 ms; ACK generation is immediate after full frame arrival. What is the cycle length in ms?
exercises.explanation: Data serialization 10 ms + outward 5 + ACK serialization 1 + return 5 =21 ms.

topics.name: Shared-medium access and Ethernet
topics.description: Compare contention strategies and reason about collisions.

skills.name: Compare access protocols
skills.description: Explain ALOHA, persistent CSMA and scheduled contention.

skills.name: Trace Ethernet collision handling
skills.description: Use round-trip propagation, minimum frames and random backoff.

lesson.title: Why sensing is not enough
paragraphs: Pure ALOHA sends when ready; a frame is vulnerable to overlapping starts over two frame times. Slotted ALOHA aligns starts and halves that vulnerable interval. In the ideal Poisson-attempt model throughput is G*exp(-2G) and G*exp(-G), respectively, where G includes retransmissions. Maxima are 1/(2e) and 1/e, not guarantees for arbitrary traffic.

CSMA senses the carrier but propagation means two far-apart stations can both observe idle and begin transmitting. One-persistent CSMA transmits immediately when idle; nonpersistent CSMA waits randomly after finding busy; p-persistent CSMA transmits with probability p in an idle slot. Token and bitmap methods avoid data collisions by allocating turns; binary countdown resolves contention using dominant bits but needs an explicit priority/fairness rule.

lesson.title: Classic Ethernet timing
paragraphs: In half-duplex shared Ethernet, CSMA/CD stops on a detected collision, sends a jam and retries after randomized backoff. To detect a worst-case distant collision before finishing, frame serialization must last at least the round-trip propagation time. Thus L_min>=2*p*R in the simplified model. Full-duplex switched Ethernet has no shared-medium collisions and does not need CSMA/CD contention.

After collision number j, the textbook binary exponential model chooses K uniformly from 0 through 2^j-1, subject to the protocol's cap, then waits K slots. At j=3 there are eight choices; two independent stations choose the same backoff with probability 1/8. State any cap and timing convention; do not transfer Wi-Fi's freeze/resume behavior into every Ethernet example.

exercises.title: ALOHA vulnerable period
exercises.prompt: Frames have duration T. In ideal pure ALOHA, another start can collide if it occurs within what total vulnerable interval around a tagged frame's start?
exercises.explanation: Starts up to T before or T after the tagged start can overlap its transmission.

exercises.title: Slotted throughput optimum
exercises.prompt: Under the ideal Poisson-attempt model, slotted ALOHA throughput is S(G)=G*exp(-G). At what offered load G is it maximized?
exercises.explanation: S'(G)=exp(-G)(1-G), which changes from positive to negative at G=1.

exercises.title: Minimum frame bits
exercises.prompt: In a simplified half-duplex collision domain, maximum one-way propagation is 20 microseconds and rate is 10,000,000 bits/s. Ignoring other constraints, what minimum frame length in bits covers round-trip propagation?

exercises.title: Backoff choice count
exercises.prompt: After the third collision, use uncapped binary exponential backoff K in {0,...,2^3-1}. How many possible K values are there?
exercises.explanation: The inclusive set 0 through 7 contains eight values.

exercises.title: Repeated collision chance
exercises.prompt: Two stations independently choose uniformly from backoff slots 0 through 7. What is the probability their chosen values coincide?
exercises.explanation: Eight matching ordered pairs exist among 64 equally likely pairs.

exercises.title: Carrier sensing limitation
exercises.prompt: Explain why two CSMA stations can collide even though each senses idle before sending.
exercises.explanation: A newly transmitted signal takes time to propagate. A distant station can begin during that interval before detecting the first signal, so the transmissions overlap.
rubric: Identify finite propagation time.
Describe simultaneous local idle observations.
Explain why sensing alone cannot eliminate collisions.

exercises.title: Binary countdown winner
exercises.prompt: Three stations contend with identifiers 010,101,100. They send most-significant bit first; 1 dominates 0, and a station sending 0 withdraws upon observing 1. Which identifier wins?
exercises.explanation: 010 withdraws at the first bit. 101 and 100 tie until the last bit, where 101 dominates.

exercises.title: Duplex distinction
exercises.prompt: Must two hosts on separate full-duplex switch ports run CSMA/CD to avoid colliding with each other? Explain the relevant physical distinction from a shared hub.
exercises.explanation: No. Full-duplex point-to-point links separate the directions and collision domains; a hub repeats transmissions onto a shared half-duplex medium. Congestion at switch output queues can still occur.
rubric: Identify full-duplex dedicated links.
Contrast a hub's shared medium.
Do not confuse absence of collisions with absence of congestion.

topics.name: Wireless access, learning switches and spanning trees
topics.description: Trace local delivery in wired and wireless LANs.

skills.name: Reason about wireless contention
skills.description: Use hidden/exposed terminals, RTS/CTS and frozen backoff.

skills.name: Trace switch forwarding
skills.description: Learn source locations, flood unknowns and prevent layer-two loops.

lesson.title: Wireless observers see different media
paragraphs: Hidden terminals cannot hear one another but can both reach a common receiver, so their transmissions may collide there. An exposed terminal hears a sender and defers even though transmission to another receiver could have succeeded. Wireless collision detection during transmission is difficult, motivating avoidance and acknowledgments rather than assuming Ethernet-style collision detection.

RTS/CTS reserves a transmission opportunity: stations hearing a relevant reservation defer for its duration, often recorded in a network allocation vector. RTS messages can still collide; the mechanism reduces expensive data collisions rather than eliminating every collision. In the simplified CSMA/CA countdown model, a station decrements in idle slots, freezes when busy, and resumes after the required idle interval.

lesson.title: Learning and loop prevention
paragraphs: A learning switch records source MAC -> ingress port when a frame arrives. It forwards a known destination to its learned port, filters it if that port equals the ingress, and floods an unknown destination to other forwarding ports in the VLAN. Learning from the destination would be wrong because an arriving frame does not prove where its recipient is.

Redundant links can create broadcast/unknown-unicast loops because ordinary Ethernet frames lack an IP-style hop limit. Spanning Tree selects a loop-free forwarding topology while retaining redundant physical links for recovery. In an ideal connected active tree of n switches there are n-1 active inter-switch edges. Infrastructure Wi-Fi uses an access point; ad-hoc communication need not. Wireless frames may distinguish immediate transmitter/receiver addresses from original source/destination.

exercises.title: Hidden terminals
exercises.prompt: A and C cannot hear one another, but both can reach B. A transmits to B; C senses idle and also transmits to B. Name the problem and explain where collision occurs.
exercises.explanation: This is the hidden-terminal problem. C's local idle observation does not describe conditions at B, where the signals overlap.
rubric: Name hidden terminals.
Locate interference at the common receiver.
Explain the mismatch between local sensing and receiver conditions.

exercises.title: Frozen countdown
exercises.prompt: A simplified Wi-Fi backoff starts at 5 idle slots. Two idle slots elapse, then the medium is busy for ten slots. After the required interframe wait, how many idle countdown slots remain?
exercises.explanation: Only the two idle slots decrement the counter; the busy period freezes it at 3.

exercises.title: RTS is not magic
exercises.prompt: Does RTS/CTS guarantee collision-free wireless communication? Give one concrete remaining collision scenario.
exercises.explanation: No. Two senders can transmit RTS to the same receiver at once, corrupting the requests; they then back off and retry. Avoidance reduces some collisions rather than proving absence.
rubric: Reject an absolute guarantee.
Describe a valid collision scenario such as simultaneous RTS.

exercises.title: First unknown unicast
exercises.prompt: An empty-table switch has four ports in forwarding state in one VLAN. A unicast frame enters port 1 with an unknown destination. On how many ports does it flood the frame?
exercises.explanation: Flood all forwarding ports except the ingress: ports 2,3,4.

exercises.title: Source learning
exercises.prompt: A frame from MAC A to MAC B arrives on switch port 3. Which table entry does backward learning establish?
exercises.explanation: The source's location is evidenced by the ingress port. The destination location is not learned from this arrival.

exercises.title: Same-port destination
exercises.prompt: A frame enters port 2, and the switch already knows its destination is also on port 2. What does ordinary learning-switch forwarding do?
exercises.explanation: The destination is on the ingress segment, so forwarding through other ports is unnecessary.

exercises.title: Spanning tree edges
exercises.prompt: A connected active spanning tree contains seven switches. How many active inter-switch edges does it contain?
exercises.explanation: A tree on n vertices has n-1 edges, so 7-1=6.

exercises.title: Why loops persist
exercises.prompt: Explain how a loop of learning switches can repeatedly circulate a broadcast frame, and how spanning tree addresses the cause.
exercises.explanation: Each switch floods broadcasts to other forwarding ports; a physical cycle returns copies that are flooded again. Spanning tree blocks selected links for forwarding so the active topology is acyclic.
rubric: Describe repeated flooding around a cycle.
Mention the lack of an ordinary Ethernet hop limit.
Explain removing active cycles rather than removing all physical redundancy.

topics.name: IP addressing, headers and configuration
topics.description: Read prefixes and distinguish network-layer roles.

skills.name: Calculate address blocks
skills.description: Use prefix masks, aligned ranges and longest-prefix matching.

skills.name: Interpret IP configuration
skills.description: Explain DHCP, IPv4/IPv6 header fields and hop limits.

lesson.title: Prefixes name aligned blocks
paragraphs: An IPv4 /p prefix fixes p of 32 bits, leaving 2^(32-p) addresses in its block. For ordinary IPv4 multiaccess subnet exercises, excluding all-zero and all-one host parts gives 2^(32-p)-2 usable host addresses; /31 and /32 have special uses, so that subtraction is not universal. A /26 boundary occurs every 64 addresses in the final octet.

Worked example: 192.0.2.77/26 belongs to 192.0.2.64/26, whose full range is .64 through .127. Its ordinary usable range is .65 through .126. Route aggregation requires contiguous aligned blocks and a valid common next hop or routing policy; two arbitrary /24s cannot simply be called a /23.

lesson.title: Headers and configuration
paragraphs: IPv4 addresses are 32 bits; IPv6 addresses are 128 bits. IPv4 IHL counts 32-bit words, whereas total length counts bytes including the header. TTL is decremented at forwarding to bound looping. IPv6's base header is 40 bytes, uses a hop limit and next-header field, and omits the IPv4 header checksum; extension headers carry optional functions.

DHCP can lease an address and supply subnet, default-router and resolver information. Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge describe a common initial exchange; not every renewal repeats all four messages. The default router reaches other IP networks, while DNS resolves names. An autonomous system is an administrative routing domain, and an Internet exchange enables participating networks to exchange traffic; neither is a layer of the OSI stack.

exercises.title: Prefix size
exercises.prompt: How many total IPv4 addresses are in a /27 block? Include network and broadcast addresses in the count.
exercises.explanation: Five host bits remain, so 2^5=32 addresses.

exercises.title: Ordinary host capacity
exercises.prompt: Under the ordinary multiaccess IPv4 convention excluding network and directed-broadcast addresses, how many host addresses does a /26 subnet have?
exercises.explanation: Six host bits give 64 total addresses; subtract the two reserved endpoints.

exercises.title: Find the network
exercises.prompt: Which prefix contains address 192.0.2.77 when using mask /26?
exercises.explanation: /26 blocks start at 0,64,128,192; 77 lies in 64 through 127.

exercises.title: Header length units
exercises.prompt: An IPv4 packet has IHL=6 and total length 1000 bytes. How many payload bytes does it contain?
exercises.explanation: IHL 6 means 6*4=24 header bytes, leaving 1000-24=976 payload bytes.

exercises.title: Hop limit handling
exercises.prompt: A router receives an IPv4 packet with TTL=1 that must be forwarded. What should happen under normal IP forwarding?

options.text: Discard because its hop budget expires; normally report ICMP Time Exceeded

exercises.explanation: Forwarding would exhaust TTL, so the packet is discarded. ICMP reporting has exceptions and rate limits.

exercises.title: IPv6 size
exercises.prompt: How many bytes are in a 128-bit IPv6 address?
exercises.explanation: 128 bits divided by 8 bits per byte gives 16; this is the address size, not the full header size.

exercises.title: Aligned aggregation
exercises.prompt: Assuming the same next hop and policy, aggregate 198.51.100.0/24 and 198.51.101.0/24 into the single exact covering prefix.
exercises.explanation: The contiguous pair starts on an even /24 boundary and shares 23 leading bits, totaling 512 addresses.

exercises.title: Configuration roles
exercises.prompt: A host knows its own IP address but no default router and no DNS server. Explain separately which missing setting affects remote IP reachability and which affects ordinary name resolution.
exercises.explanation: A default router provides a next hop for destinations without a more specific local route. A DNS resolver translates names; an already known IP address does not itself require DNS lookup.
rubric: Separate routing from naming.
Explain the default route's scope.
Avoid claiming DNS forwards application packets.

topics.name: Routing algorithms and forwarding
topics.description: Compute routes and explain convergence and policy.

skills.name: Run routing updates
skills.description: Apply Bellman-Ford and Dijkstra to specified link costs.

skills.name: Explain routing behavior
skills.description: Distinguish forwarding, convergence, longest prefixes and policy.

lesson.title: Local vectors versus a topology map
paragraphs: Distance vector uses D_x(d)=min_v[c(x,v)+D_v(d)] over neighbors v. A router adds the cost to each neighbor to that neighbor's advertised distance, then chooses the minimum. Advertisements can become stale, causing loops and count-to-infinity after failures; information that a route is gone can propagate slowly.

Link-state routing floods local adjacency information so routers can build a topology map and run Dijkstra for nonnegative link costs. Start with source distance zero, settle the smallest tentative distance, and relax adjacent edges. Record predecessors or first hops as well as distances. Flooding link-state information is not the same as broadcasting every data packet.

lesson.title: From routing decisions to packet forwarding
paragraphs: Forwarding applies a routing table to one packet; routing constructs and updates that table. Longest-prefix matching chooses the most specific matching entry, regardless of the textual order of entries. An explicit default route /0 applies when nothing more specific matches.

Worked example: edges A-B=2, A-C=7, B-C=1, C-D=2, B-D=8 give shortest A-D path A-B-C-D with cost 5. Distance vector learns such results through neighbors, while link state derives them from the map. Inter-domain BGP uses path-vector information and policy; shortest numerical path is not a universal description of its route selection. Including an AS path helps detect a path containing one's own AS.

exercises.title: Distance-vector update
exercises.prompt: Router X reaches neighbor A at cost 2 and B at cost 5. A advertises distance 7 to D; B advertises 1. What minimum distance should X compute to D?
exercises.explanation: Compare 2+7=9 through A with 5+1=6 through B.

exercises.title: Dijkstra path cost
exercises.prompt: An undirected graph has A-B=2,A-C=7,B-C=1,C-D=2,B-D=8 and no other edges. Find the minimum A-to-D cost.
exercises.explanation: A-B-C-D costs 2+1+2=5, less than A-C-D=9 or A-B-D=10.

exercises.title: Longest matching prefix
exercises.prompt: Routes are 10.0.0.0/8 -> A, 10.2.0.0/16 -> B, 10.2.3.0/24 -> C, default -> D. Which next hop serves 10.2.3.9?
exercises.explanation: All three prefixes match, but /24 is the longest and most specific.

exercises.title: Count to infinity
exercises.prompt: After a destination fails, two distance-vector routers keep advertising paths to it through each other. Explain why costs can rise gradually instead of immediately becoming unreachable.
exercises.explanation: Each mistakes the neighbor's stale route for an independent path and adds its link cost. Their circular dependency repeatedly increases the metric until a configured infinity or new information breaks it.
rubric: Identify stale advertisements.
Explain circular next-hop dependence.
Connect each update to an increment in cost.

exercises.title: One relaxation
exercises.prompt: In Dijkstra's algorithm, settled node B has distance 4. Edge B-C costs 3, and C's tentative distance is 10. What is C's updated tentative distance?
exercises.explanation: Relax with min(10,4+3)=7.

exercises.title: Routing versus forwarding
exercises.prompt: Classify (a) running Dijkstra after a topology update and (b) looking up a packet's destination prefix to choose an output interface.
exercises.explanation: (a) is route computation in the control plane; (b) is packet forwarding using the resulting table.
rubric: Identify routing as table construction/update.
Identify forwarding as per-packet use of that table.

exercises.title: AS-path loop
exercises.prompt: AS 65010 receives a proposed BGP route with AS path 65020,65030,65010. Why should it reject this path for ordinary loop prevention?
exercises.explanation: Its own AS appears in the path, indicating the route would loop through a domain already traversed. Path-vector information reveals a dependency that a distance alone would hide.
rubric: Locate AS 65010 in the advertised path.
Explain the routing-loop concern.

exercises.title: Policy is not hop count
exercises.prompt: Why might an inter-domain router prefer an AS path of length four over an available path of length two? Give a policy-based reason.
exercises.explanation: Local policy can favor a customer route, contractual relationship or other preferred route before AS-path length is compared. BGP is not pure shortest-hop routing.
rubric: Give a plausible administrative/economic policy.
Explain that policy can outrank AS-path length.

topics.name: Fragmentation, ARP, ICMP and NAT
topics.description: Trace packets across MTUs and address boundaries.

skills.name: Calculate fragmentation
skills.description: Respect per-fragment headers, eight-byte offsets and DF/MTU behavior.

skills.name: Trace address translation and control
skills.description: Explain next-hop ARP, NAT mappings and ICMP diagnostics.

lesson.title: Fragment payload, not the entire packet
paragraphs: An MTU constrains the complete IP packet on a link. With an IPv4 header of H bytes, nonfinal fragment payloads must fit floor((MTU-H)/8)*8 bytes. Offsets count original payload bytes in units of eight. Each fragment gets a header; the identification associates fragments, and MF indicates more fragments follow. Reassembly normally occurs at the destination.

Worked example: a 2020-byte IPv4 packet with 20-byte header carries 2000 payload bytes. MTU 1020 allows payloads 1000 and 1000, total lengths 1020 each, offsets 0 and 125, MF 1 then 0. If DF forbids fragmentation, a router cannot simply ignore it. IPv6 routers do not fragment; path-MTU feedback enables the source to choose suitable packet sizes.

lesson.title: Different addresses solve different problems
paragraphs: To reach a remote IPv4 network over Ethernet, a host ARPs for its next-hop router's MAC, not normally the remote host's MAC. ARP resolves an on-link IPv4 address into a link address. ICMP reports conditions such as time exceeded or an MTU problem; traceroute varies hop limits to elicit hop-by-hop replies, but missing replies do not prove a router is absent.

Port-translating NAT maps an internal address/port tuple to an external tuple, rewrites headers and relevant checksums, and remembers how to reverse the translation for replies. Two internal hosts can share an external IP because their mappings use distinct external ports. NAT complicates unsolicited inbound connections; translation itself is not a substitute for an explicitly configured firewall or encryption.

exercises.title: Fragment count
exercises.prompt: An IPv4 packet has total length 2020 bytes and a 20-byte header, with DF=0 and no options. Outgoing MTU is 1020 bytes. Using maximum valid payload sizes, how many fragments are needed?
exercises.explanation: The payload is 2000 bytes and each fragment can carry 1000, which is divisible by eight.

exercises.title: Offset units
exercises.prompt: An IPv4 fragment begins 1000 bytes into the original IP payload. What integer goes in its fragment-offset field?
exercises.explanation: Offsets are in units of eight payload bytes: 1000/8=125.

exercises.title: Round payload down
exercises.prompt: IPv4 MTU is 600 bytes and every fragment has a 20-byte header. What is the largest valid payload size in bytes for a nonfinal fragment?
exercises.explanation: The raw capacity is 580 bytes; round down to a multiple of eight: floor(580/8)*8=576.

exercises.title: Complete fragment layout
exercises.prompt: A 1500-byte IPv4 packet with 20-byte header and DF=0 crosses MTU 600. No options; maximize nonfinal payloads. Give each fragment's payload size, total length, offset and MF flag.
exercises.explanation: Original payload 1480 splits as 576,576,328. Total lengths are 596,596,348; offsets 0,72,144; MF flags 1,1,0. All offsets refer to the original payload.
rubric: Subtract the original header first.
Use 576-byte nonfinal payloads.
Give all three total lengths and offsets.
Set MF only on nonfinal fragments.

exercises.title: DF at a smaller MTU
exercises.prompt: An IPv4 router must forward a packet larger than its outgoing MTU, but DF=1. What is the normal response?

options.text: Drop and normally send ICMP fragmentation-needed feedback

exercises.explanation: DF prohibits router fragmentation. MTU feedback allows the sender to adapt; ICMP delivery is not guaranteed.

exercises.title: Which address to ARP
exercises.prompt: Host 192.0.2.10/24 sends to 198.51.100.20 via default router 192.0.2.1. Its ARP cache is empty. Which IPv4 address does it normally ARP for?
exercises.explanation: The remote destination is off-link; the Ethernet frame must reach the local next-hop router.

exercises.title: NAT reply mapping
exercises.prompt: NAT maps internal 10.0.0.2:5000 to external 203.0.113.9:40000 for a connection. A matching reply arrives at the external tuple. Explain the destination rewrite and the table information needed.
exercises.explanation: The NAT finds the applicable protocol/connection mapping and rewrites the reply destination to 10.0.0.2:5000, updating relevant checksums. The mapping disambiguates the intended internal endpoint.
rubric: State both rewritten address and port.
Use the saved mapping rather than guessing the internal host.
Mention checksum consistency.

exercises.title: Traceroute silence
exercises.prompt: A traceroute probe receives no reply at one hop, but later-hop replies arrive. Does that prove the silent router drops all forwarded traffic? Explain.
exercises.explanation: No. A router may filter or rate-limit ICMP responses while forwarding data; the reply path may also lose a response. Later replies show that some probes reached farther hops, but only a stable-path assumption would establish that they crossed the same silent router.
rubric: Separate control-message response from data forwarding.
Give a plausible reason for silence.
Use later-hop evidence without claiming a unique diagnosis or a necessarily identical route.

topics.name: UDP, TCP sequencing and connection state
topics.description: Trace transport identities, byte numbers and failure handling.

skills.name: Use transport services
skills.description: Distinguish sockets, ports, datagrams, byte streams and checksums.

skills.name: Trace TCP state and numbering
skills.description: Account for SYN/FIN, cumulative ACKs, retransmission and old duplicates.

lesson.title: Processes, datagrams and streams
paragraphs: IP identifies network endpoints while transport ports help select processes. A TCP connection is distinguished by local/remote addresses and ports (with protocol context), so a server port can serve many clients. Server socket workflows commonly bind, listen and accept; a client connects. Sending through a socket does not prove that a remote application has committed a transaction.

UDP preserves datagram boundaries but provides no built-in retransmission, ordering or congestion-control service. TCP provides an ordered byte stream and therefore does not preserve application message boundaries. Both use checksums over transport information and an IP pseudoheader; checksum detection is not a guarantee against every corruption and is not cryptographic authentication.

lesson.title: Byte numbers and control flags
paragraphs: A TCP sequence number identifies the first data byte in a segment. A cumulative ACK names the next byte expected, acknowledging the contiguous prefix before it. SYN and FIN each consume one sequence number; a pure ACK consumes none. Retransmitting the same bytes reuses their numbers. All arithmetic is modulo 2^32 in actual TCP, though examples below stay far from wraparound unless stated.

Worked trace: client ISN=100 sends SYN; first data begins at 101. After 40 contiguous data bytes, the peer ACKs 141. FIN at 141 is acknowledged by 142. Three-way establishment confirms both initial sequences; teardown permits independent closing of the directions. Timers, packet lifetimes and sequence-space reuse matter because an old duplicate must not be mistaken for new data; textbook clock-based forbidden-region diagrams illustrate this constraint, not the complete modern ISN algorithm.

exercises.title: After SYN
exercises.prompt: A TCP client sends SYN with sequence number 100 and no payload. What sequence number labels its first data byte? No wraparound occurs.
exercises.explanation: SYN consumes one sequence number.

exercises.title: Cumulative acknowledgment
exercises.prompt: A receiver expects byte 501 and receives one in-order TCP segment containing 200 bytes, with no SYN or FIN. What ACK number should it send?
exercises.explanation: Bytes 501 through 700 arrived, so the next expected byte is 701.

exercises.title: Out-of-order data
exercises.prompt: A TCP receiver cumulatively ACKs 1000, meaning it next expects byte 1000. A segment starting at 1200 with 100 bytes arrives while bytes 1000-1199 remain missing. Ignoring SACK fields, what ACK number remains appropriate?
exercises.explanation: Later data do not fill the gap in the contiguous byte prefix.

exercises.title: Third segment sequence
exercises.prompt: TCP ISN is 20. After the SYN, a sender transmits data segments of 30,50,70 bytes with no gaps or other flags. What sequence number starts the third segment?
exercises.explanation: First data starts at 21; adding the first two payloads gives 21+30+50=101.

exercises.title: Pure ACK consumption
exercises.prompt: A pure TCP ACK has no data, SYN or FIN. How many sequence numbers does it consume?
exercises.explanation: The ACK flag alone does not occupy sequence space.

exercises.title: UDP length
exercises.prompt: A UDP datagram has a 100-byte application payload. Its standard UDP header is 8 bytes. What value goes in the UDP length field, in bytes?
exercises.explanation: UDP length includes UDP header and payload, but excludes the IP header.

exercises.title: Message boundaries
exercises.prompt: An application makes two TCP send calls of 100 bytes each. Must the receiving application obtain two reads of 100 bytes? Explain how it should identify messages.
exercises.explanation: No. TCP exposes a byte stream; reads can split or combine the bytes. The application needs its own framing, such as fixed lengths, a length prefix or an escaped delimiter.
rubric: Reject correspondence between send calls and reads.
Explain stream semantics.
Offer an unambiguous application framing method.

exercises.title: Sequence-space lifetime
exercises.prompt: A toy protocol has 256 byte-sequence labels and sends continuously at 64 bytes/s. Old packets may survive 5 seconds. Explain the risk of cycling through the labels without an additional protection mechanism.
exercises.explanation: Labels wrap after 256/64=4 seconds, shorter than the 5-second lifetime. An old packet can remain when its label is reused and be mistaken for current data unless extra state or timing rules distinguish it.
rubric: Compute four seconds to wrap.
Compare with five seconds of possible lifetime.
Explain ambiguity rather than claiming guaranteed corruption on every run.

topics.name: Flow control, congestion and transport limits
topics.description: Distinguish receiver protection from network protection and trace specified control models.

skills.name: Calculate sending limits
skills.description: Combine advertised and congestion windows with bytes in flight.

skills.name: Trace congestion and failures
skills.description: Apply stated Tahoe/Reno rules and explain end-to-end limits.

lesson.title: Two separate bottlenecks
paragraphs: The receiver window rwnd protects receive-buffer capacity; the sender's congestion window cwnd limits offered load to the path. An idealized sender can have at most min(rwnd,cwnd) bytes outstanding. To find new data it may send now, subtract already outstanding bytes. A window-limited throughput ceiling is window/RTT, further limited by link capacity, losses and application behavior.

Routers can signal congestion through loss or ECN marking; end hosts respond by reducing sending. Queue management such as RED may drop early to avoid persistent full queues. Flow control alone cannot prevent congestion in an intermediate router, and a large receiver buffer does not imply spare network bandwidth.

lesson.title: State the congestion-control variant
paragraphs: In round-based textbook slow start with one ACK per segment and no losses, cwnd roughly doubles each RTT until the threshold. Congestion avoidance increases about one MSS per RTT. Tahoe resets cwnd to one MSS after loss; simplified Reno recovers near half after triple duplicate ACKs but resets after timeout. Exact real implementations differ, so traces below state the algorithm and threshold conventions.

TCP delivery cannot by itself guarantee exactly-once application effects after crashes: an operation may execute before its reply is lost. Applications need durable identifiers/state for such guarantees. TCP also delays later stream bytes behind a missing byte; independent QUIC streams reduce cross-stream transport head-of-line blocking, although losses still consume capacity and can delay bytes within a stream. These conceptual contrasts do not replace implementation-specific protocol documentation.

exercises.title: New bytes permitted
exercises.prompt: cwnd=12000 bytes, rwnd=8000 bytes, and 3000 bytes are outstanding. In the idealized window model, how many additional bytes may be sent now?

exercises.title: Window-limited throughput
exercises.prompt: A fixed 20,000-byte window limits a lossless connection with RTT=0.1 seconds. Ignoring all other limits and overhead, what throughput ceiling in bytes/s follows?
exercises.explanation: Window/RTT=20000/0.1=200000 bytes/s.

exercises.title: Slow-start rounds
exercises.prompt: In an ideal round-based slow-start model cwnd starts at 1 MSS and doubles after every completed RTT. No loss or threshold is encountered. What is cwnd after three completed RTTs, in MSS?

exercises.title: Tahoe after loss
exercises.prompt: Use the course's simplified Tahoe rule: on loss set ssthresh to half the current cwnd and cwnd to 1 MSS. If cwnd was 16 MSS, what is the new ssthresh in MSS?
exercises.explanation: Half of the stated current window is 16/2=8 MSS; cwnd itself resets separately to 1.

exercises.title: Reno recovery model
exercises.prompt: Use a simplified Reno model that sets the post-recovery cwnd to half the pre-loss cwnd after triple duplicate ACKs. If it was 20 MSS, what is post-recovery cwnd? Ignore temporary fast-recovery inflation.
exercises.explanation: The prompt's multiplicative decrease is 20/2=10 MSS; it is not a timeout case.

exercises.title: Receiver versus path
exercises.prompt: A receiver advertises a large buffer, but a router on the path is overloaded. Explain why rwnd alone cannot solve this and what cwnd contributes.
exercises.explanation: rwnd represents endpoint storage, not intermediate queue capacity. cwnd adapts to path congestion signals to constrain the load even when the receiver can accept more data.
rubric: Identify which resource rwnd protects.
Identify which resource congestion control protects.
Connect congestion feedback to sending reduction.

exercises.title: Crash after an operation
exercises.prompt: A server commits a payment operation, then crashes before the client receives its reply. The client retries over a new TCP connection. Why does TCP reliability not prevent duplicate execution? Propose an application-level safeguard.
exercises.explanation: TCP does not make the database effect and reply one atomic operation across crashes. Use a stable request identifier and atomically commit the payment effect with a durable request/result record, so a retry reuses the original outcome. An equivalent downstream idempotency guarantee is needed when the effect is outside that transaction.
rubric: Separate transport delivery from application commit.
Identify uncertainty after a lost reply.
Require atomic persistence of the effect and deduplication/result record, or an equivalent downstream idempotency guarantee.

exercises.title: Head-of-line scope
exercises.prompt: Explain how independent QUIC streams can reduce head-of-line blocking compared with carrying multiple application streams in one TCP byte stream, and name a remaining limitation.
exercises.explanation: Missing bytes in one TCP stream delay later bytes for every multiplexed application stream. QUIC can deliver other streams independently of a gap in one stream. Loss still affects congestion capacity, and ordered delivery within the affected stream can still wait.
rubric: Explain TCP's shared ordered byte stream.
Explain independent stream delivery.
State a remaining loss or within-stream limitation.

topics.name: Cryptographic building blocks
topics.description: Practice toy arithmetic while distinguishing secrecy, integrity and authentication.

skills.name: Calculate toy cryptographic operations
skills.description: Trace RSA, substitutions, permutations and block chaining.

skills.name: Match security properties
skills.description: Distinguish hashes, MACs, signatures and encryption.

lesson.title: Different primitives, different promises
paragraphs: Encryption aims at confidentiality; integrity/authentication require an appropriate authenticated construction. A cryptographic hash is unkeyed, a message authentication code uses a shared secret, and a digital signature uses a private signing key with public verification. An unkeyed checksum or CRC detects accidental errors but does not stop an attacker who can recompute it.

A substitution box maps bit patterns; a permutation box reorders bit positions. In CBC encryption C_i=E_K(P_i XOR C_(i-1)), with C_0 the IV. Decryption applies D_K first and then XORs the previous ciphertext. The toy examples specify the complete transformation; they are not secure ciphers. CBC alone does not authenticate data, and secure IV/padding/authentication handling is outside these arithmetic exercises.

lesson.title: RSA and key agreement as arithmetic
paragraphs: Toy RSA chooses primes p,q, n=pq, phi(n)=(p-1)(q-1), and exponents e,d satisfying e*d=1 modulo phi(n). Encrypt m as m^e mod n and decrypt as c^d mod n for an encoded message in the modulus range. With p=3,q=11,e=3, phi=20 and d=7. Real RSA requires large keys and standardized padding; tiny textbook calculations are only demonstrations.

Diffie-Hellman participants exchange g^a and g^b modulo a suitable prime, deriving g^(ab). Agreement alone does not authenticate the peer: an active intermediary can conduct separate agreements unless identities and transcripts are authenticated. Always distinguish the arithmetic shared-secret property from the surrounding protocol's authentication guarantees.

exercises.title: Toy RSA modulus
exercises.prompt: For a toy RSA example p=5 and q=11. What is modulus n?

exercises.title: Toy RSA inverse
exercises.prompt: Toy RSA uses p=3,q=11,e=3. Find the smallest positive d satisfying e*d=1 modulo phi(n).

exercises.title: Toy RSA encryption
exercises.prompt: Encrypt integer m=4 in toy RSA with n=33,e=3. What is c=m^e mod n?

exercises.title: Toy CBC first block
exercises.prompt: A deliberately insecure 4-bit toy cipher is E(x)=x XOR 0011. CBC uses IV=0101 and first plaintext block 1110. What is the first ciphertext block?
exercises.explanation: First XOR plaintext with IV: 1110 XOR 0101=1011. Apply E: 1011 XOR 0011=1000.

exercises.title: Permutation box
exercises.prompt: A P-box outputs input positions (3,1,4,2), numbering the four input bits left to right from 1. What is its output on 1010?
exercises.explanation: Input positions 3,1,4,2 contain 1,1,0,0.

exercises.title: CRC against an attacker
exercises.prompt: A sender appends a CRC to a message but uses no secret. Explain why an active attacker who can replace the message can generally also produce a passing CRC.
exercises.explanation: The CRC algorithm is public and unkeyed; the attacker can compute the checksum of the replacement. Accidental-error detection does not provide adversarial integrity.
rubric: Identify absence of a secret/authentication property.
Explain recomputation on replacement data.
Distinguish detection from authentication.

exercises.title: Diffie-Hellman toy secret
exercises.prompt: Toy Diffie-Hellman uses p=23,g=5. Alice's exponent is 2; Bob sends public value 10. Compute Alice's shared value 10^2 mod 23.
exercises.explanation: 100=4*23+8, so the residue is 8.

exercises.title: Public verification
exercises.prompt: A publisher wants recipients to verify a software message using a public key, without sharing the publisher's secret. Which primitive fits that verification goal?

options.text: A shared-key MAC with its key made public

exercises.explanation: Sign with the private key and verify with the public key, whose authentic association with the publisher must also be established.

topics.name: Network security and trust boundaries
topics.description: Explain what TLS, VPNs, Tor and application security do and do not hide.

skills.name: Analyze protected channels
skills.description: Identify endpoints, intermediaries and metadata visibility.

skills.name: Choose and interpret controls
skills.description: Explain firewall state, authentication factors and key lifecycle.

lesson.title: Protection has endpoints
paragraphs: TLS authenticates peers according to its certificate/key configuration and protects traffic between its endpoints. A browser must validate the expected server identity, not merely see some certificate. Traffic timing, packet sizes and some routing metadata can remain visible. Do not treat the lecture's simplified handshake diagram as a universal message count across all TLS versions and resumption modes.

A VPN tunnel protects traffic to the VPN endpoint, which becomes a trust boundary. A commercial VPN can observe information at that boundary; it does not automatically replace end-to-end HTTPS. Tor distributes knowledge across relays: a guard sees the client, an exit sees the outward destination and may see plaintext application data without end-to-end encryption. A single relay's view differs from an adversary correlating both ends; anonymity is not an absolute guarantee.

lesson.title: Controls and key lifecycle
paragraphs: A stateless packet filter inspects fields independently; a stateful firewall can track established flows; deeper inspection examines additional content when accessible. Encryption can limit inspection without endpoint cooperation. Wireless WEP examples illustrate that weak constructions and reused key material can defeat goals even when a system is labelled encrypted; the lesson is the mechanism, not deployment advice from old slides.

MFA combines evidence from distinct factor categories, such as knowledge and possession; two passwords are still one category. DNSSEC authenticates signed DNS data when validated but does not encrypt DNS traffic. PGP combines message encryption and signatures; OTR-style messaging emphasizes forward secrecy and deniability, unlike permanently verifiable signatures. Forward secrecy aims to protect older session contents if a long-term key is later compromised, assuming ephemeral secrets were erased and the protocol's conditions held.

exercises.title: TLS endpoint identity
exercises.prompt: A browser receives a cryptographically valid certificate for other.example when connecting to intended.example. Is a valid signature alone enough to authenticate the intended server? Explain.
exercises.explanation: No. The certificate must also authenticate the requested identity through the relevant name checks and trusted chain. A certificate for another name does not establish intended.example.
rubric: Distinguish a valid signature from identity binding.
Require matching the intended hostname and appropriate trust validation.

exercises.title: VPN endpoint visibility
exercises.prompt: A user tunnels plaintext HTTP through a VPN to a website. Which statement is correct about the VPN exit after tunnel decryption?

options.text: It cannot observe HTTP content because a VPN was used
It can observe the plaintext HTTP content
It automatically creates end-to-end TLS to the website

exercises.explanation: Tunnel encryption ends at the VPN endpoint. The application traffic remains plaintext unless separately protected.

exercises.title: A Tor guard's view
exercises.prompt: Assume an ordinary three-relay Tor circuit, no endpoint compromise, no collusion or global traffic correlation. What does the guard directly know that the exit need not know?

options.text: The full circuit's destination by definition

exercises.explanation: The client connects to the guard. Layered encryption limits that relay's direct knowledge of the later path and contents under the stated threat model.

exercises.title: Stateful filtering
exercises.prompt: Explain how a stateful firewall can allow replies to an outbound TCP connection while rejecting an unrelated unsolicited inbound SYN.
exercises.explanation: It records allowed connection state and tuples, then matches return traffic to that state. A new inbound SYN has no such matching allowed connection and is evaluated under the new-connection policy.
rubric: Use stored connection state and endpoint/protocol information.
Distinguish replies from new connection attempts.
Avoid claiming all packets with an ACK flag are automatically trustworthy.

exercises.title: Factor categories
exercises.prompt: Which pair combines distinct authentication factor categories?

options.text: Password and a hardware security key

exercises.explanation: A password is knowledge; a hardware key demonstrates possession. Two memorized secrets remain the same factor category.

exercises.title: DNSSEC scope
exercises.prompt: Does validated DNSSEC by itself hide the requested domain from an observer of plaintext DNS packets? Explain the security property it supplies.
exercises.explanation: No. DNSSEC authenticates signed DNS data and its integrity through validation; it does not encrypt the query or response transport.
rubric: Reject confidentiality from DNSSEC alone.
Identify authenticity/integrity as the relevant properties.

exercises.title: Forward secrecy
exercises.prompt: An attacker records encrypted sessions and later steals a server's long-term signing key. Explain the intended benefit of forward secrecy and one necessary qualification.
exercises.explanation: Past session keys should not be recoverable solely from that later long-term-key compromise. This depends on suitable ephemeral key agreement and erasure of session secrets; compromise during the session is a different threat.
rubric: Identify protection of past sessions.
Limit the claim to the stated later compromise.
Mention ephemeral-secret handling or another valid condition.

exercises.title: Onion encryption order
exercises.prompt: A client wants relays guard, middle, exit to remove one encryption layer each in that order. Which key must form the outermost layer?
exercises.explanation: Encrypt the exit layer first, then middle, then guard. The guard must be able to remove the outermost layer it receives.

topics.name: DNS, email and the web
topics.description: Trace name resolution and application-level exchanges.

skills.name: Trace application protocols
skills.description: Differentiate recursive/iterative DNS, mail delivery and web requests.

skills.name: Calculate encoding and request costs
skills.description: Use Base64 grouping and stated HTTP timing assumptions.

lesson.title: Names and mail routes
paragraphs: DNS organizes a hierarchical namespace with delegations and resource records. A recursive resolver pursues an answer on a client's behalf; iterative exchanges can return referrals to another server. Caching uses TTL to reduce repeated work, so a lookup need not contact the root each time. DNS is not limited universally to UDP; the lecture's common-case explanation should not become an absolute transport rule.

SMTP transfers/submits email; IMAP provides mailbox access and synchronization, while MIME describes message content and attachments. Base64 encodes three input bytes (24 bits) as four six-bit alphabet indices. It is encoding, not encryption. With padding and no line breaks, n bytes require 4*ceil(n/3) characters; one leftover byte yields two '=' symbols, two leftover bytes one.

lesson.title: Web requests and reusable connections
paragraphs: A URL identifies scheme, authority and resource path. HTTP request methods express application operations and status codes report outcomes; HTML describes document content. Persistent connections amortize setup across requests. Pipelining and multiplexing are different ways to carry concurrent work; their ordering and transport blocking depend on the HTTP and transport versions.

Worked timing model: without DNS, TLS or transfer time, a fresh TCP connection takes one RTT to establish and an HTTP request/first response another RTT. Sequentially retrieving three objects over one persistent connection therefore takes four RTTs under that deliberately simple model; three separate sequential connections take six. Real page loading includes parallelism, resource dependencies and transfer sizes, so assumptions are part of the answer.

exercises.title: Mail protocol role
exercises.prompt: Which protocol is principally responsible for transferring email between mail servers?
exercises.explanation: SMTP transfers mail; IMAP accesses a mailbox, and ARP resolves local link addresses.

exercises.title: Iterative referral
exercises.prompt: A DNS server responds with information about another server to ask, rather than resolving the entire name on the client's behalf. Which behavior is illustrated?
exercises.explanation: A referral directs the querying resolver to the next relevant name server.

exercises.title: Base64 length
exercises.prompt: Encode 10 bytes using padded Base64 with no line breaks. How many output characters, including '=', result?
exercises.explanation: 4*ceil(10/3)=4*4=16 characters.

exercises.title: Base64 padding count
exercises.prompt: A padded Base64 encoding contains exactly two input bytes. How many '=' padding characters appear?
exercises.explanation: Sixteen input bits produce three alphabet characters after zero-padding the final sextet, plus one '=' to complete four characters.

exercises.title: Persistent HTTP timing
exercises.prompt: Ignore DNS, TLS and transmission time. A fresh TCP handshake costs one RTT; each sequential object request/response costs one RTT. Three objects use one persistent connection. How many RTTs elapse in this model?
exercises.explanation: One setup RTT plus three sequential request RTTs gives four.

exercises.title: DNS cache lifetime
exercises.prompt: A resolver caches a record with TTL 300 seconds. After 120 seconds, with no refresh or invalidation, how many seconds of TTL remain?
exercises.explanation: 300-120=180 seconds before this cache entry's original TTL expires.

exercises.title: Encoding is not secrecy
exercises.prompt: An email attachment is Base64-encoded but otherwise unencrypted. Explain whether someone who can read the encoded message can recover the attachment.
exercises.explanation: Yes. Base64 is a public reversible representation and needs no secret key; it adapts binary data to text-oriented transport rather than providing confidentiality.
rubric: Identify public reversibility.
Distinguish encoding from encryption.

exercises.title: One web navigation
exercises.prompt: Outline the roles of DNS, TCP, TLS and HTTP for a simplified fresh HTTPS-over-TCP request with an uncached hostname. Do not specify version-dependent handshake packet counts.
exercises.explanation: DNS obtains destination address information; TCP establishes an ordered byte stream; TLS authenticates the server and protects the channel; HTTP carries the resource request and response inside that channel.
rubric: Give each protocol its distinct role.
Order the dependencies sensibly for the stated fresh connection.
Do not equate DNS or TCP establishment with server identity validation.

topics.name: Streaming, CDNs and peer-to-peer lookup
topics.description: Connect user experience to buffering, distribution and overlay routing.

skills.name: Reason about delivery and QoE
skills.description: Calculate buffering and explain CDN placement and perceived quality.

skills.name: Trace distributed lookup
skills.description: Use BitTorrent roles and Chord successor/finger rules.

lesson.title: Delivery rate and experience
paragraphs: A playback buffer absorbs variable arrival times but adds startup or interactive delay. Stored media can prefetch farther ahead than live media; interactive conversations impose tighter latency constraints. If a stream plays at b bits/s, B buffered bits cover B/b seconds during a complete arrival outage. Sustained arrival below playback rate eventually drains the buffer.

CDNs replicate/cache content near demand and direct users toward an appropriate node. DNS-based redirection can reflect the recursive resolver's location rather than perfectly locating the client; load and availability also matter. Quality of experience is a user-centered outcome, not simply raw bitrate. Subjective mean-opinion scores and objective models have different strengths and limitations; compression, stalls, latency and context all affect perceived quality.

lesson.title: Peers and a structured key space
paragraphs: BitTorrent divides content into pieces whose hashes support integrity checking; peers exchange pieces, while a tracker or DHT helps discover peers. A tracker need not store the content itself. Piece-selection and reciprocal uploading policies influence availability and incentives; hashing is useful only relative to a trusted expected identifier.

In an m-bit Chord ring, keys and node identifiers lie modulo 2^m. A key belongs to its first clockwise node, its successor. Finger i starts at n+2^i modulo 2^m for i=0,...,m-1 and points to that start's successor. To route a lookup, use the closest preceding finger when the key is not in the immediate successor interval; do not overshoot the key merely because a finger is numerically close. Ideal logarithmic lookup assumes maintained routing state; churn requires stabilization and redundancy.

exercises.title: Buffered playback
exercises.prompt: A stream consumes 2,000,000 bits/s. Its buffer contains 10,000,000 bits and arrivals stop completely. Ignoring decoding effects, how many seconds until the buffer empties?
exercises.explanation: Buffered time=10,000,000/2,000,000=5 seconds.

exercises.title: Persistent rate deficit
exercises.prompt: Playback consumes 4 Mb/s while arrivals sustain 3 Mb/s, with decimal rates. A buffer starts with 12 megabits. How many seconds until depletion if rates stay constant?
exercises.explanation: The net drain is 1 megabit/s, so 12 megabits last 12 seconds.

exercises.title: CDN and resolver location
exercises.prompt: A CDN steers clients using the location of the DNS resolver issuing the query. Explain why a client using a distant recursive resolver might receive a suboptimal CDN node.
exercises.explanation: The resolver's location may differ from the client's. A node close to that resolver can have a longer or slower path to the actual client, so the location proxy is imperfect.
rubric: Distinguish resolver from end client.
Connect the mismatch to node selection and path quality.

exercises.title: Key ownership
exercises.prompt: A 4-bit Chord ring has nodes 1,4,9,12. A key belongs to the first node clockwise at or after it. Which node owns key 10?
exercises.explanation: The successor of identifier 10 among the present nodes is 12.

exercises.title: Wraparound successor
exercises.prompt: In the same 4-bit ring with nodes 1,4,9,12, which node owns key 15 under the clockwise successor rule?
exercises.explanation: There is no node at 15 or before wraparound 16, so the next clockwise node is 1.

exercises.title: Finger-table entry
exercises.prompt: A 4-bit Chord ring has nodes 1,4,9,12. Node 4's finger with zero-based i=2 starts at (4+2^2) mod 16. Which node is stored in that finger?
exercises.explanation: The finger starts at 8; successor(8)=9.

exercises.title: Tracker versus content peer
exercises.prompt: In a tracker-based BitTorrent design, explain the tracker's role and why downloading a peer list does not itself download the requested file.
exercises.explanation: The tracker provides information about peers participating in a swarm. File pieces are transferred from peers; discovery metadata and content transfer are separate functions.
rubric: Identify peer discovery as the tracker role.
Identify peers as piece suppliers.
Distinguish metadata from content.

exercises.title: QoE tradeoff
exercises.prompt: Two streaming systems deliver the same average bitrate. One starts immediately but repeatedly stalls; the other buffers briefly and then plays smoothly. Explain why equal bitrate does not imply equal quality of experience, including the tradeoff for interactive calls.
exercises.explanation: Startup delay and stall frequency affect perceived quality independently of average bitrate. Buffering can improve continuity for stored video, but extra latency can disrupt turn-taking in interactive communication.
rubric: Identify at least two experience factors beyond bitrate.
Explain the buffer-versus-stall tradeoff.
Distinguish interactive latency requirements from stored playback.
